sources.entry: Anki-fy Your Life gets into why it makes sense to invest in your memory.

summary.title: Anki-fy Your Life
summary.one_liner: Using Anki spaced-repetition flashcards to move important facts, book notes and hard research concepts into long-term memory so your brain can connect them when solving problems.
keywords: how much time to memorize a fact
michael nielsen augmenting long term memory
takeaways: Long-term memory is effectively unlimited; the bottleneck is how fast information moves from working memory into storage.
Anki can be used beyond rote learning: store key facts, book highlights and conversation notes as cards so the brain can make connections over them.
Roughly 15-20 minutes a day is said to be enough to build a 10,000-card database, and each extra fact costs about 5-10 minutes of time.
Michael Nielsen's rule of thumb: memorize a fact if it seems worth 10 minutes of future time, and always memorize facts that seem striking.
For hard research papers, build understanding by writing many basic-to-complex questions and re-reading, as Nielsen did with the AlphaGo paper.
summary.summary: The article argues that human long-term memory is effectively limitless and that storing important information there, rather than relying only on search, lets the brain build schemas and make subconscious connections. It proposes using Anki, a spaced-repetition flashcard tool, to memorize key facts, notes from books, conversations and videos, and to understand hard research papers by asking progressively harder questions. It draws heavily on Michael Nielsen's essay Augmenting Long Term Memory and Nicholas Carr's The Shallows, and it links to a separate guide on writing effective flashcards.
